items.title: Help us make image_transport and point_cloud_transport better for Makoa!
items.summary: Hi all, I’m not a maintainer of neither image_transport nor point_cloud_transport, though I’m their big user and proponent (point_cloud_transport has, in the end, origins in my lab , though it has come a long way since then). The more I use both throughout various ROS 2 distros, the more obstacles and surprises I keep hitting. I’ve started putting together a list of issues/API differences/API inconveniences of both: Unify the APIs of image_transport and point_cloud_transport in Makoa? · Issue #434 · ros-perception/image_common · GitHub . My ultimate goal would be to sync the API of both and make it easy to use in both Python and C++. I’d like to get it as easy as changing rclcpp::Publisher for image_transport::Publisher with minimum required code changes and with as many features as the normal publisher/subscriber has (like connect callbacks). Ideally, before Makoa Mata-mata code-freeze (May '27). Do you agree this is something worth resolving? (there will be some API-level friction caused by this). Do you see any other issues not mentioned in my Github post? Please add them! The proposed timeline is collecting inputs until mid November and then start with the implementation. 1 pos

items.articleText: Gazebo PMC Meeting Minutes 2026-10-19 - Gazebo PMC - Open Robotics Discourse Gazebo PMC Meeting Minutes 2026-10-19 Gazebo Gazebo PMC gazebo , meeting , pmc azeey October 20, 2026, 9:03pm 1 Hi Gazebo Community! This week’s meeting was held on 2026-10-19T18:00:00Z and the following is a summary: PMC Business Approved adding Luca Della Vedova as a mentee PMC member. New agenda items Community Meeting : A reminder for this week’s community meeting on Scalable Multi-Robot Simulation in ROS 2 and Gazebo , featuring multi-robot simulation, namespaces, and automatic bridging. Please note the change in date and time this month (7:00 PM Pacific) to better accommodate the Asia-Pacific region. Fuel Server Outage & Maintenance : The Fuel server experienced downtime over the weekend due to high memory consumption triggered by crawler traffic downloading models in parallel. The server was restarted, and backend changes are being prepared to avoid loading full models into RAM along with an updated deployment mechanism (fuel-server#25 ). Auto-Merge & Required CI Checks : Maintainers are reminded to verify which CI checks are required before enabling GitHub auto-merge. A recent Fortress backport (gz-sim#4076 ) auto-merged despite failing builds because only the DCO check was required, and had to be reverted (gz-sim#4079 ). Branch protection rules are being updated in terraform_github_repos#10 to require Jenkins and GitHub Actions CI checks. Lightweight 2D Physics Engine Exploration (Box2D vs. TPE) : Discussed experimenting with Box2D as a physics engine plugin to support very large-scale planar simulations with hundreds of robots requiring only collisions and basic kinematic motion. Compared against the existing Trivial Physics Engine (TPE), which currently lacks joint support; a deeper comparison between Box2D and extending TPE will be conducted. Updates Simulation, Physics & C++20 Migration Bullet-Featherstone Kinematic Mode : Merged the full set of PRs enabling kinematic mode in Bullet-Featherstone on Rotary, with backports planned after verification on a demo world: Enforce position limits on kinematically driven joints (gz-physics#1118 ) Fix toggling links between kinematic and dynamic (gz-physics#1122 ) Kinematic base velocity for links with a CoM offset (gz-physics#1123 ) Fix force-torque sensor in hybrid kinematic/dynamic modes (gz-physics#1124 ) Fix root joint position and velocity (gz-physics#1125 ) ECM Batch Queries : Merged runtime-typed EntityComponentManager (ECM) batch queries and exposed them to Python (gz-sim#4006 ). C++20 Migration : Continuing work on gz-cmake#580 to avoid hardcoding the C++ standard so builds follow the exported target standard. PRs are in review for sdformat examples (sdformat#1733 ), gz-sim plugin examples and tutorials (gz-sim#4086 ), and the DART ContactSurface check in gz-physics (gz-physics#1134 ). Rendering, Sensors & Transport Ogre 1.12 Migration : The large Ogre 1.12 migration PR was split into stacked PRs for easier review (gz-rendering PRs ). While general custom shaders were fixed, custom terrain heightmap shaders remain broken due to upstream class removals in Ogre 1.12; the PMC agreed to merge without custom terrain shader support if a quick fix is not found, and request examples from users if needed later. PixelBuffer API Adaptations : Backports adapting gz-sensors to the PixelBuffer API (gz-sensors#674 ) have been merged for Harmonic and Fortress, and are in review for Jetty (gz-sensors#677 ) and Ionic (gz-sensors#678 ) ahead of upcoming point releases. Zenoh CI in gz-sim : A PR is in review to run Ubuntu Resolute CI tests a second time using Zenoh on gz-sim main (gz-sim#4085 ). The team agreed that gz-transport should fail explicitly when Zenoh is selected via environment variable but not compiled in, rather than silently falling back to ZeroMQ. Web & Documentation Gazebo Web Ecosystem : Ongoing work to modernize the gazebosim-app web frontend (gazebosim-app PRs ). We are also evaluating the feasibility of rewriting gzweb in Rust using the Bevy engine to improve performance, realism, and modern SDFormat support. Maintainer Guidelines : Merged documentation updates covering backport timing, downstream testing tradeoffs, and prerelease version bump review policies (docs#723 ). Infrastructure, Packaging & Release Tooling macOS 26 (Tahoe) & Homebrew : Tahoe bottling is in progress (homebrew-simulation#3599 ). The primary hurdle is compiling ogre1.9 without the Apple Graphics Library (AGL, removed in macOS 26), for which a community contributed patch is in review (homebrew-simulation#3615 ). Investigated flaky Homebrew build failures on Harmonic and Fortress caused by a Doxygen bug (homebrew-simulation#3616 ); mitigation is complete for Harmonic and in review for Fortress. Pixi on macOS : Prerequisites for supporting Pixi on macOS are in review (release-tools#1566 , release-tools#1568 ). Discussed the possibility of eventually phasing out Homebrew bottle builds if Pixi provides a smooth macOS developer experience, while keeping the Homebrew tap available. Release & CI Tooling : An automated changelog generation tool is up for review (release-tools#1447 ). A PR to skip Linux CI-pr Jenkins jobs when modified files match an ignore list is awaiting final updates (release-tools#1558 ). Build warning fixes are in review for gz-physics (gz-physics#1127 ) and gz-cmake (gz-cmake#603 ). rosdistro-extension work is underway to generate binary packages for testing distributions and handle automatic sourcing of setup.bash from child to parent workspaces. As always, the meeting notes are available at Gazebo PMC meeting weekly agenda - Google Docs . items.articleText: Battle Drones—a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer Simon Willison’s Weblog Newsletter Sponsored by: Teleport — AI agents (and sub-agents they spawn) are given the same access as humans, but they never sleep. Learn how to monitor and constrain their behavior with isolated ephemeral trusted runtimes. Battle Drones—a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer 20th October 2026 My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I’m somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to “Make it a LOT more fun”. It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here’s what I’ve built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. Here’s a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units—all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes—temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode —red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode —one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events—it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath —a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A “Daily Op” challenge Ranks and achievements (Medals ) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded—I’ve reviewed almost none of the code, and it’s built in a language (TypeScript) that I’ve hardly used myself. I’ve playtested it quite a bit though, and it’s been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here’s a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here’s a shared transcript . I’d given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here —it looked like this: It’s recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn’t any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn’t even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version (try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the “AI vs. AI” mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI’s image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn’t much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here —it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn’t very fun to play though—I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can’t actually make something that’s genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs “dynamic workflows”, described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn’t get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. You can try v4 here —it looks like this: I had Claude write its own release notes —here are the highlights: Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that’s losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play. Openers : pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts. Call-down powers : Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike. Objectives and salvage : Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap. Feel : combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer. Command : battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement. New modes : Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign. Progression : heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op. Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%. Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features. v5: Battle Drones goes 3D After the success of Ultracode at “Make it a LOT more fun”, I decided to be more ambitious: Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version : The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code. v6 (play v6 here ) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7 ) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a “Condor” troop carrying aircraft. v8: Archipelago I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game—it really had been a case of me saying “make it more fun” and “add visual polish” for the past few releases. I’d noticed that the AI didn’t use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often—there wasn’t a great strategic reason to use them. It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map. This resulted in my longest prompt yet: Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles. To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor. Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board. The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places I want to encourage a battle over uplinks. The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications You get to design a new biome for this The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It’s definitely the most fun map to play, once you’ve got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting—it now looks like this: v10: Goliath, and agent battles I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game—think Jaegers from Pacific Rim , or Titans from Warhammer 40,000. Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude: Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be. Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale. Supported models: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Supported features: Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification SWA bounded replay Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler) Batch-invariant inference Deterministic sampling Structured outputs Feature details and configuration Optimized kernels: FlashMLA , DeepGEMM , DeepEP , TileKernels , DeepSelect , and custom TileLang kernels . DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification: accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1 ; DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE controls the maximum draft length (default: 5). Decoder SWA bounded replay: reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length. items.title: Claude designed protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins
items.articleText: Related articles Claude discovers a novel enzyme system with CRISPR-like repeats View more Summary: As part of our work experimenting with how Claude can help accelerate drug discovery, we asked an internal research model to design minibinders (small proteins that attach tightly to a target) against scorpion neurotoxins. Claude worked from our prompt and four follow-ups, which we developed in collaboration with the financial investment research firm Citrini Research. Teams at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience experimentally tested 211 designs for binding. Of these, 17 met our criteria. We’re releasing all 211 designs and their data as a resource for the field. In August, we showed how Claude designed protein minibinders after being given a single prompt. A month before we released those results, a team from Citrini Research had approached us with an interesting question: could Claude (and AI drug discovery more generally) enable a group of motivated nonexperts to tackle a genuine problem in human health? Members of our life science research team set out to answer this, first by brainstorming problems with Claude. We landed on asking for Claude’s help designing novel protein binders against scorpion neurotoxins, with the hope that they could one day be used to develop a scorpion antivenom. Scorpions sting 1.2 million people or more every year, resulting in more than 3,250 deaths, mostly among children in parts of the world with limited access to medical care. New treatments are expensive to make, and are also unlikely to earn back the cost of developing them. With so little investment, scorpion envenomation has been described as a neglected tropical disease. We started by giving Claude the same prompt we’d used in our earlier protein-binder study, after modifying it with Citrini.1 Over the next 64 hours, an internal research model, operating within Claude Science, worked mainly autonomously, although we directed its work with four follow-ups. Under our supervision, Claude analyzed the research data, generated the figures, and drafted the final report. Claude’s design campaign produced 17 protein binders that each bind to one of four scorpion neurotoxins that are known to be dangerous to humans. Throughout the process, Claude generated 318,484 protein designs and selected 180 of them for testing. Our team added 31 more, with Claude’s help. Our partners at Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience, two contract research organizations (CROs), lab-tested all 211 designs to see if they would bind to the toxins they were designed against, and 17 designs met our criteria for a binder. We have not confirmed whether these binders neutralize scorpion venom in a cellular environment, so we do not claim to have produced an antivenom. We sent Claude’s work to two outside experts, Susana Vázquez Torres and Timothy P. Jenkins, who said they felt this work was a promising first step. If AI can now design credible binders against several hard-to-target toxins in days and they can be confirmed in the lab within weeks, this could, in theory, speed up discovery for envenomation and other neglected diseases. The challenge, as always, is turning those binders into safe, affordable, and widely accessible drugs. We share more detail in our technical report , and are making all 211 designs and their data available . Designing a binder against almost any target no longer seems unrealistic. We can now obtain very tight binders remarkably quickly, and binding itself is no longer the main bottleneck. For venomous animals such as snakes and scorpions, whose bites and stings kill or seriously injure large numbers of people, particularly in underserved regions, the real impact will come from tackling the parts of the therapeutic pipeline that go beyond binding. The challenge is to use these extraordinary tools to develop molecules that can become real drugs, ones that are safe, affordable, and widely accessible. Susana Vázquez Torres , Postdoctoral Researcher, Structural Biology Programme, Spanish National Cancer Research Centre (CNIO), Madrid, Spain. Designing de novo binders against five toxins from four species of scorpions Scorpion venom contains multiple protein neurotoxins. The neurotoxins that are most likely to harm or kill humans attach to sodium channels , large proteins embedded in the membranes of nerve cells that allow them to fire. When sodium channels are disrupted, nerves fire at the wrong time—this releases large amounts of stress chemicals, like adrenaline. In severe cases, this can cause heart failure and excess fluid buildup in the lungs, occasionally resulting in death. There are some antivenoms available for scorpion stings. They’re generally made using the antibodies of immunized animals, a process that can take months. Venom is milked from thousands of scorpions and used to immunize horses; scientists then purify the resulting antibodies from the horses’ blood. Traditional antivenoms can work when given early, but they’re usually effective for only a small number of neurotoxins. They’re also expensive to produce, and in many regions are costly or in short supply. De novo design offers a potential solution. A binder is a molecule that attaches tightly to a specific target; antibodies are one natural example. In principle, a binder that targets the part of a neurotoxin that latches onto sodium channels could stop the toxin from reaching the channel. In de novo design, protein binders are generated from scratch against a specific target. These binders are designed computationally and can be optimized for druglike properties such as potency and stability, which could make them easier to supply in regions where stings most often occur. Our approach was inspired by an earlier effort that designed de novo proteins that neutralized snake neurotoxins and protected mice. To our knowledge, no de novo -designed binders against scorpion neurotoxins have been described. For this campaign, we chose to target five scorpion-venom neurotoxins across four regions: Mexico (Cn2), Brazil (Ts1), North Africa (AaH I and AaH II), and the Middle East (LqhIII). We also chose to aim the designs at each toxin’s channel-binding site. Claude picked the toxin structures to use for design by searching the Protein Data Bank (PDB) as well as the AlphaFold database (AFDB). For each toxin, it selected five hotspots , specific amino acid positions on the toxin that its binder designs were meant to latch onto. We were primarily wondering if Claude could design binders against individual toxins. But we were also curious if Claude could design binders that targeted multiple toxins. There’s a practical reason for trying to design multitoxin binders, namely that it would reduce the number of molecules needed for a universal antivenom cocktail—which would be the most cost-effective and regionally neutral treatment. We selected these five scorpion toxins (Cn2, Ts1, AaH I, AaH II, and LqhIII) as a challenging test of multitoxin design: they share one fold for the overall shape of the protein, but any two are only 26% to 62% identical in their amino acid sequences. To see how far Claude could go, we asked it to design four kinds of binders: binders against each of the five toxins individually; binders that targeted the β-family toxins Ts1 and Cn2; binders that targeted the α-family toxins AaH II, AaH I, and LqhIII; and binders that targeted all five toxins simultaneously. Designing credible binders against five toxins in parallel, in a matter of days, is a great showcase of the AI-driven paradigm shift we are seeing in therapeutic discovery. This is especially true for neglected diseases such as animal envenomings, which have been largely starved of innovation due to low commercial incentives. Being able to agentically tackle the uniquely broad target space across animal toxins provides a significant speed-up in discovery, and brings realistic therapeutic solutions much closer. Timothy P. Jenkins , Associate Professor, Technical University of Denmark. Claude ran the design campaign with considerable autonomy Our initial prompt defined the neurotoxin targets, the protein design and folding tools, and the rules for novelty, scoring, and filtering. Beyond choosing the structures and amino acid hotspots, Claude also set the quality thresholds a design had to clear, decided how much to lean on each available design tool, and developed the strategies for designing binders against multiple toxins. Ultimately, Claude used 12 design tools to generate 318,484 designs, filtering out any that resembled a toxin or a known protein. Claude co-folded and screened 553,052 design-toxin pairs, predicting each pair’s structure as one complex. Sixty-four hours after we gave Claude our initial prompt, it produced its final list of 180 designs. The campaign used on the order of 10,000 GPU hours.2 Claude worked autonomously for 24 hours following our first prompt. Its results encouraged us to prompt Claude to continue its campaign and look for better designs. Our follow-up prompts were mainly focused on directing Claude to design a multitoxin binder. Claude selected most of the 180 designs—including our strongest binder (Cn2-B1)—only after our third follow-up. At our request, Claude sent the protein sequences to Twist Bioscience (in emails indicating they were written by Claude), which produced the proteins in order to see how well they would bind to the toxins. We later worked with Claude to add another 31 designs, increasing the total to 211 designs: 60 designs against a single toxin (12 per toxin), 30 designs against the two β-family toxins, 30 designs against the three α-family toxins, and 91 designs against all five toxins. Of the 211 designs our teams assessed, 17 met our criteria for a binder, each against a single toxin. None of the designs made against multiple toxins met our criteria for more than one. (Beyond being limited by its current capabilities, there could be many explanations for why Claude struggled with this, including our prompting, the limitations of available design tools, and even the biological feasibility of multitoxin design.) Seven designs were binders against Cn2, four against AaH II, four against AaH I, and two against LqhIII. Among the 60 single-toxin designs, 11 were binders (18%). This rate is consistent with typical protein design campaigns, including our previous work. Testing Claude's designs in the lab After completing the campaign, we sent the designs to Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience to test them for binding. Each group produced the designs in their labs, but in different formats. Adaptyv Bio expressed them in a cell-free system , which uses protein-making machinery extracted from bacteria rather than living cells. Twist Bioscience expressed the designs in mammalian cells (in this case, human kidney cells) as fusions to Fc , the stem of an antibody. These are complementary ways to measure the underlying binding process, and we combined them in order to improve confidence in our results. Both labs measured binding by surface plasmon resonance (SPR), in which a toxin flows over the design while the SPR instrument tracks in real time how quickly a toxin binds to and detaches from it. The resulting trace, called a sensorgram, produces a measurement known as the dissociation constant (KD), which is a measurement for binding strength (or affinity ). The lower the KD, the tighter the binding. When it came to evaluating the resulting designs, we set out strict criteria for labeling a design a binder against a toxin. The design needed to be a hit at both labs3 —that is, it needed to show evidence of binding against that toxin in every replicate, and every KD needed to be 1 µM or tighter. We also required that the design show no signal against CLEC12A, an unrelated human protein used to measure off-target binding or “stickiness.” Claude’s Cn2 binders likely bind the same site as a toxin-neutralizing antibody Antibodies and nan

items.title: Publish fake stats, get cited in LLMs
items.articleText: Publish stats, get cited: The tactic that put my data all over the web - Peec AI Publish stats, get cited: The tactic that put my data all over the web Metehan Yesilyurt GEO Researcher Oct 7, 2026 GEO Know-How Inside the page Want more of Peec AI? Subscribe to our weekly newsletter. Subscribe Share this What I learned about AI search when I made up 50,000 stats that got cited by ChatGPT... About 7 months ago, I launched a website with 50,000 statistics. Every one of them was fake. Google has forgotten the site exists and deindexed the pages, but ChatGPT hasn't. Since the website went live 7 months ago, it has sent more than 10,000 AI sessions its way. And now more than 330 referring domains, including Shopify, Bluehost, and DHL, link to the site. Its made-up numbers have also ended up in an academic paper and in a bank's investment research. At Peec AI and in the industry, we talk about GEO and SEO every day, and we keep looking for new tactics. I’ve been working on this stats page one for a long time, sharing pieces of it publicly along the way. Of course, it’s experimental, but the results have been hard to ignore. Where the idea for publishing fake statistics came from The impetus to seed a site with statistics came out of long-running research I've been doing on LLMs, relevance engineering, and grounding (credit to the iPullRank team, Dan Petrovic, and Wil Reynolds). In the course of my work, I noticed a pattern: as more teams write time-sensitive and breaking content with LLMs, those LLMs have to look for (seemingly) reliable data during their research to fill the gaps in their knowledge. Statistics are often exactly what they’re looking for. Most GEO advice focuses on one moment: getting your brand into the AI answer. This experiment looks at what happens after the answer, when people take that output and use it, putting it into presentations, adding it to a shopping list, and yes, publishing it on their website. I didn't come up with the idea for this experiment alone. Hat tip to Seer Interactive, who already published an eye-opening study in August 2025 that got a few thoughts bouncing around in my head. Several months later, those thoughts came together and finally made it to the top of my to-do list. In March 2026, I started working on building the site that would let me test my ideas. The setup: a website and 50,000 made-up stats, created in one day Quick context for anyone who wasn’t following along in real time as I ran this experiment: I bought a brand-new domain, stateglobe.com, and generated 50,000 statistics pages in a single day with GPT-4.1. The site purports to provide stats on SEO, content marketing, social media, e-commerce, and web technology from 200 countries. Except every number was totally invented. I never checked a single one. I pushed them to the site with a basic AI web design template. This cost me around $30. Later, I added 15,000 listicles on top of the statistics. That was about $20 more, so all in all, this is an experiment that came in at the very low price of about $50. The reaction when I first shared it was wild. When my friend Kevin featured it in Growth Memo , it reached a much bigger audience. I think people responded so enthusiastically to this work because it showed great results while also speaking to the fears people have about what ends up in AI search results. What happened Google buried the site almost immediately When I launched the site, traffic, indexing, and engagement were initially going really well. Using indexer tools, I got almost the entire site indexed within a week, and it started to appear in Google results. Then two Google updates came out right after launch, and my Google visibility collapsed. I've been invisible on Google for many months now. Indexed pages bounce between 5 and 20 impressions. At one point, I got curious and created a subdomain to see if I could increase impressions, but it didn't really help. Other than that, I haven't touched the site. Some pages might even fail to load now and then. I don't know. But when I sat down to write this, I checked the crawl data in Cloudflare after 7 months. In the last 30 days alone, the site got more than 600,000 requests from bots. Around 72,000 of them came from ChatGPT-User. That is the agent ChatGPT uses to open a page in real time while answering someone. So these are not training crawls. Each one is ChatGPT fetching a fake statistics page to answer a real question. Unlike Google, ChatGPT never stopped pulling from the site And when I say, “never stopped,” I mean ChatGPT really never stopped. After 7 months, the site now has 330+ referring domains According to Ahrefs and Semrush, the site has links from 330+ other sites. That includes well-known brands like Shopify, DHL, and Bluehost. With strong Google performance, the numbers might have been even better. ChatGPT is still citing it to this day Google may have forgotten about the site, but ChatGPT clearly hasn’t. The site is still earning citations and traffic more than 7 months after launch. If you've read Tomek's ChatGPT Index research , you're lucky, because it’s a great intro to how ChatGPT search works. If you haven't, add it to your reading list right now, because it helps explain why my website has been living in ChatGPT/OpenAI Index for so long. A completely made-up website still performing so well is shocking. Since March, GA4 shows 10,000+ sessions from ChatGPT alone, and Cloudflare shows the site has high marks for retrieval. I didn’t include direct sessions in overall visits, because it mostly looks like bot traffic. Remember the dead internet theory! Right after I joined Peec in June 2026, I also set up a visibility dashboard in our tool to track a few prompts. Performance for them is still strong. On October 7, stateglobe.com was ranked second for visibility on these prompts, behind only data powerhouse Statista. Retrieval is not ranking The constant retrieval is the first big lesson: ranking on Google and being retrievable by an LLM are two different problems. When ChatGPT searches, it doesn't just copy Google's top 10. It rewrites your prompt into its own sub-queries (called fanout queries), pulls candidates from its search sources and its own cache, reranks them, and then opens a handful of pages to ground the answer. A page can be invisible on Google and still perform well in every one of those LLM steps. StateGlobe is a good example. While Google dropped it, the AI retrieval bots kept coming back. For GEO, this means Google rankings are only one signal, not the whole picture. If you only track Google, you are missing a channel that can work even when Google says “no.” Fake data turned into real citations You’d expect that if a site performs well with information retrieval tools, its information would begin to appear out in the wild. And you would be right. StateGlobe was built entirely on fake data, using the cheapest model available and a prompt that was nothing more than a list of countries and topics plus two sentences. Nevertheless, the output was… …cited in an academic paper… …used in investment research by Qatar's largest financial group… …cited by an economics publication in India… …and used as a source in a research report from a Canadian influencer community. Note that these are only the citations that linked back to the StateGlobe site. Presumably, many more used the data without a link. The uncomfortable implication: citation laundering On day one, a fake number on StateGlobe had zero authority. It was a random stat on a brand-new domain. Then an academic paper cited it. Then a bank. Now the next person, or the next model, that finds this number sees a stat with a source. And that source is cited by serious institutions. The fake data certainly didn't become true, but every citation made it look more trustworthy. It has the potential to get worse: after so much retrieval and citation, these pages end up in web crawls, and web crawls end up in training data (I hope it hasn’t!). A number that started as a GPT-4.1 guess can become something the next model "knows." This points to the larger risk suggested by this experiment, and it's why I'm sharing this as research, not as a playbook for fake content. Verifying sources should become an essential part of writers’ and researchers’ workflows. Lastly, we tried running our experiment with real data Once I began working at Peec, I decided to try a version of this test again. As the GEO Research team, we talked through the results up until that point and quickly launched a simple new page. This time, there were no made-up numbers, and we checked every stat and properly cited its source. You can view it here: peec.ai/ai-search-geo-statistics . Almost immediately, sites we suspect use AI to write their content started linking to us. For the second time, using a second site, earning links by publishing statistical content proved that a hypothetically strong tactic worked in reality. Lessons learned Why publishing statistics leads to LLM citations The two tests show that LLMs have a strong preference for seeking out statistics when asked to write articles. The mechanism is simple: More and more content is written with LLMs. When an LLM writes, it researches the appropriate topic. When the LLM hits a gap, it looks for a number to fill it. The reasons behind this process are equally clear. Research means fanout queries asking for statistics When a prompt requires research, the model breaks it into sub-queries, adds modifiers like "statistics," "data," "report," or the current year (if also requested in the prompt text). If someone asks for the model to compose a blog post about remote work, the model will search for "remote work statistics 2026." Pages that optimize for what models search rather than for what humans type will appear more often in LLM results. A number looks like evidence that can fill knowledge gaps When a model is asked to draft a piece of writing, a citation to a page that says "Remote work is growing" adds little authority and remains vague. If that page instead says "X% of employees work remotely at least once a week," there’s suddenly something that is specific, quotable, and additive. When a model grounds an answer, a specific number is the most useful thing it can find. These numbers look like evidence, though as this experiment proves, sometimes they aren’t. The model doesn’t check the number A search-grounded piece of LLM-written content has a tight budget for latency and cost. The system fetches a few pages, pulls the relevant passages, and starts to write. Fact-checking doesn’t happen anywhere in the process. Verifying a single statistic would mean finding independent sources, comparing them, and resolving conflicts. Across billions of prompts by millions of users, the costs in both time and money would add up, making verification too slow and too expensive for practical purposes. To get around this, LLMs use rerankers that score relevance, but not truth. That means if a passage matches the query and looks authoritative, it gets used. Statistics have a built-in freshness that models like I've written before about ChatGPT's recency bias in how it scores sources. Statistics pages contain the year in the title, the headings, and the URL. Three built-in signals to the model that what’s on the page is fresh. How to build a statistics page the right way The two tests I ran show that statistics pages are a very powerful way to get your content cited by LLMs. While I absolutely do not recommend coming up with bogus data, you can use the learnings from our small test to create your own pages with real data. Here's what worked for us at Peec and what I would do if I were making a statistics page again. Make one claim per sentence. Each stat should make sense on its own, out of context. Retrieval doesn’t work on pages, but rather on passages. If a number needs the paragraph above it to make sense, it probably won't get pul

items.articleText:
## Verify Docker Image Signature

All LiteLLM Docker images are signed with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/). Every release is signed with the same key introduced in [commit `0112e53`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0).

**Verify using the pinned commit hash (recommended):**

A commit hash is cryptographically immutable, so this is the strongest way to ensure you are using the original signing key:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/0112e53046018d726492c814b3644b7d376029d0/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.106.1
```

**Verify using the release tag (convenience):**

Tags are protected in this repository and resolve to the same key. This option is easier to read but relies on tag protection rules:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/v1.106.1/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.106.1
```

Expected output:

```
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - The signatures were verified against the specified public key
```

---

items.title: Reservoir launches new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers
items.summary: Reservoir hopes to put agricultural robotics startups to work in the orchards, vineyards and berry fields alongside researchers and growers. The post Reservoir launches new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Reservoir opened Reservoir Farms – Salinas, its flagship innovation hub. | Source: Reservoir Reservoir, Washington State University’s Prosser Irrigated Agriculture Research and Extension Center (IAREC), the Washington Tree Fruit Research Commission (WTFRC), and the Tri-City Development Council (TRIDEC) today announced a new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers. The site will put agricultural robotics startups to work in the state’s orchards, vineyards and berry fields alongside researchers and growers. The announcement comes as Washington growers face rising labor costs and a shrinking workforce for some of the hardest crops in the world to automate. These include apples, cherries, pears, blueberries, wine grapes, and hops. Reservoir is an agricultural innovation center and venture capital fund. The organization is focused on helping agtech startups succeed where agriculture happens, in the field. Reservoir started its innovation center in the Salinas Valley. It hopes to expand to other key regions across California and the American West. Reservoir VC backs startups solving real problems in high-value crops and the rugged physical AI stack. More about Reservoir’s innovation center Earlier this year, the company officially opened Reservoir Farms – Salinas, its flagship on-farm innovation hub for specialty crops. The new site features multiple innovation barns and 24 acres of dedicated commercial test fields. This creates the most concentrated ecosystem of technology leaders, growers, and startups anywhere in agriculture to rapidly scale solutions for global food production challenges. More than 300 growers, agricultural leaders, federal and state officials, community partners, investors and media attended the grand opening of Salinas site. “From our early days, Reservoir listened intently to partners to understand where innovation in agriculture was stuck,” said Danny Bernstein, founder and CEO of Reservoir. “Once our vision to create an on-farm innovation center was clear, we worked relentlessly with partners across the industry to bring the energy, focus and skills necessary to manifest the space and people necessary to make this a reality. With the doors open, the focus turns to execution and impact – in the form of real-world solutions for growers, upskilled jobs for rural communities, and a more secure food supply for American consumers.” Last summer, Reservoir announced plans to expand its on-farm innovation center model across California, Arizona, and other major growing regions. Each hub will be anchored by leading academic and research and developmnt institutions. As part of this multi-region strategy, Reservoir invited startups to run pilots over the winter months at the University of Arizona’s Yuma Agricultural Center. The startups gained the opportunity to test technologies in commercial desert vegetable production. In August, Reservoir announced a $10 million, three-year R&D partnership with John Deere . The partnership aims to accelerate real-world development and commercialization of rugged AI technologies for high-value crop agriculture. It builds on a relationship that began when Reservoir was founded in 2024. Deere said the partnership with Reservoir reflects its “commitment to an innovation ecosystem that moves faster from prototype to grower impact.” Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness! items.title: RoboBusiness rebrands as Robotics Summit & Expo West
items.summary: Robotics Summit & Expo West sharpens focus on deploying robotics and AI in the real world, complementing the East Coast flagship event. The post RoboBusiness rebrands as Robotics Summit & Expo West appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Arrowfly , an award-winning B2B media and marketing company, today announced that RoboBusiness , the leading robotics industry event for the past 20 years, is being rebranded as Robotics Summit & Expo West, a conference and expo dedicated to the design, deployment, and scaling of commercial robots and businesses. The first event under the new name will be in October 2027 in Santa Clara, Calif. The timing reflects how the industry has matured. Many robotics companies have moved past the prototype stage, shipping real products into factories, warehouses, and other sites. The questions that define their work are no longer only technical. They are about design for manufacturing, bringing products to market, implementation, managing growing fleets, and providing service and support. Robotics Summit & Expo West will help industry professionals meet increasing demand for intelligent systems across sectors. “The robotics industry has matured, and the hardest problems have grown with it,” said Steve Crowe, executive editor of The Robot Report and chair of the Robotics Summit. “For 20 years, RoboBusiness brought this community together. Robotics Summit & Expo West will serve that community by sharing lessons from industry leaders on how to move from a pilot that works to a product deployed across multiple sites and building a business that can support it.” Robotics Summit & Expo West is organized around the questions that define the post-prototype stage of a robotics company: Deployment at scale: What changes when a robot moves from a controlled pilot to multiple live sites, including integration, fleet management, remote monitoring, and autonomous operations in increasingly unstructured environments. Go-to-market and commercial strategy: How robotics companies are responding to market demand and structuring pricing, sales, and channel strategies for products that combine hardware, software, and services. Field data and product decisions: How real-world performance data flows back into product iteration and AI model evolution. Ongoing service and support, whether directly or through partners, is also key to demonstrating a return on investment. Investment and growth: How investors evaluate robotics companies, and how founding teams can build businesses that last. The conference program includes keynotes with industry and thought leaders, sessions focused on the latest technical and business topics, insightful panel discussions, and a curated expo floor. Attendees can learn from the founders, operators, and investors who are shaping the future of robotics. One mission. Two conversations The rebrand clarifies Arrowfly’s robotics event portfolio. Robotics Summit & Expo Boston (June 2–3, 2027, John B. Hynes Convention Center), the flagship East Coast show, focuses on the core technical and engineering challenges of building robotic systems. Robotics Summit & Expo West focuses on scaling the product and the company behind it. Together, the two events serve the full lifecycle of designing, building, and bringing a robotics product to market. “Deployment does not end the development process. It changes who is asking the questions,” said Amanda Buehner, senior vice president of sales & strategy, engineering, at Arrowfly. “The engineer designing a new mobile robot and the operations leader managing robots across a warehouse network are both essential to this industry. They need different conversations. That is what the Robotics Summit lineup now provides.” Robotics hardware, software, and solution providers looking to reach the engineers, product leaders, and executives scaling robotics can learn about sponsorship and exhibit opportunities by contacting Arrowfly’s robotics team. About Arrowfly Arrowfly is a live and digital B2B destination serving professionals across the engineering, healthcare, food, retail, and hospitality sectors. Across 40+ brands, the company delivers trusted journalism, original content, live and digital events, video, and demand generation programs to the decisionmakers shaping their industries. Powered by Clara, Arrowfly’s proprietary performance platform, partners get real-time visibility into audience engagement, lead quality, and campaign ROI. The company is backed by an established reputation for editorial independence and credibility across the markets it serves. For more information, visit arrowfly.com. Media Contact Annie Wissner VP of Marketing, Arrowfly [email protected] About The Author Steve Crowe Steve Crowe is Executive Editor, Robotics, WTWH Media, and chair of the Robotics Summit & Expo and RoboBusiness. He is also co-host of The Robot Report Podcast, the top-rated podcast for the robotics industry. items.title: 2027 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards open nominations
items.summary: The TRR50 winners will be celebrated at an awards gala during the Robotics Summit & Expo, which will be held on June 2-3, 2027 in Boston. The post 2027 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards open nominations appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: Aaron Parness, director of applied sciences at Amazon Robotics, and Bhavana Chandrashekhar, the senior manager of applied science at Amazon Robotics, speaking at the 2026 RBR50 gala. The Robot Report is seeking nominations for its 2026 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards. The RBR50 has recognized the most innovative organizations and robots since 2012, and this year we’re rebranding to The Robot Report 50 (TRR50). Here are the winners from 2026 , 2025 , 2024 , 2023 , 2022 , and 2021 . Each year, The Robot Report selects the most interesting and important robotics innovations from around the world. The deadline for submissions is Friday, Jan. 5, 2027 . Submit your nomination(s) below. The TRR50 winners will be celebrated at an awards gala during the Robotics Summit & Expo , which will be held on June 2 and 3, 2027 in Boston. Some of the winners will also be demoing their robots on the Robotics Summit expo floor in the TRR50 Pavilion. TRR50 Awards categories To be eligible, all nominations must be for innovations that were initiated, released, or executed between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31, 2026. The TRR50 is looking for submissions in the following categories: Startup of the Year: The nominee must be less than five years, and it must be already testing its innovation with customers. Last year, Physical Intelligence, which offers AI models that change how robots learn, earned the Startup of the Year award , and the year before, Mytra took home the honors. Application of the Year: The winner will be a use case that has previously been difficult to automate and where robotics and automation have demonstrated a clear benefit over previous processes. Last year, Harvard University won for its wearable robot aids to help those struggling after a stroke or with ALS. The year before, TEPCO won for its work to remove radioactive fuel from Japan’s Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant. Robot of the Year: The TRR50 awards are seeking a robot that is a game-changer in terms of technology innovation, use case, and industry influence. Amazon’s Vulcan robot won the award in 2026, and Robotaxi developer Waymo won in 2025 . Robots for Good: The TRR50 Robots for Good Award honors a robot that make a positive impact on society by addressing social challenges, improving quality of life or work, or promoting sustainability. Tatum Robotics won in 2026 for its robotic hand that enables tactile sign language communication. In 2025, Hello Robot’s Stretch 3 mobile manipulator won the inaugural Robots for Good Award . Best use of AI: The TRR50 Best Use of AI Award will honor a real-world application for AI in robotics. This new category will highlight one use case that exemplifies how AI is changing robotics. Products: This category honors new robots, enabling technologies, and research. Business: This category honors major milestones, unique business models, and other initiatives positioning a company as a market leader. Applications: The TRR50 will also recognize innovations that improve productivity, quality, and cost-effectiveness, as well as those that automate new tasks. For any questions related to the 2027 TRR50 Robotics Innovation Awards, please contact Steve Crowe . report.one_sentence_summary: Gazebo 및 ROS 2 코어 런타임 인프라 변경과 DeepSeek의 대규모 추론 프레임워크 DeepInfer 오픈소스 공개, OpenAI의 바이오 기업 인수 소식이 전해졌습니다.
report.section_robotics:
- **Gazebo PMC 회의록**: Rotary에서 Bullet-Featherstone의 기구학(kinematic) 모드를 활성화하는 PR 세트가 병합되어 데모 월드 검증 후 백포트될 예정이며, 런타임 타입 EntityComponentManager(ECM) 배치 쿼리가 병합되어 Python에 노출되었습니다 [4].
- **ROS PMC 회의록**: Windows 10 지원 종료에 따라 Jazzy와 Humble 배포판의 Windows 환경 빌드팜 CI가 건너뛰어지도록 변경되었으며, ROS 2 Rolling 배포판에서 libstatistics_collector 패키지가 제거되었습니다 [5].
report.section_devtools:
- **DeepSeek DeepInfer**: 대규모 프로덕션 서빙을 지원하는 오픈소스 고성능 오프라인 추론 프레임워크로 DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash 모델을 지원하며, 지원 하드웨어는 NVIDIA SM100 GPU와 화웨이 Ascend 950 NPU입니다 [11].
- **Anthropic Python SDK v1.17.0**: 조직 웹훅 엔드포인트 및 사용자 프로필 적용 이벤트가 추가되었고, Bedrock 및 Mantle 클라이언트의 default_headers에 워크스페이스 ID가 유지되도록 수정되었습니다 [14].
report.section_industry:
- **OpenAI의 Orchestra Bio 인수**: OpenAI가 생명과학 R&D에 AI 기반 운영을 도입하고 신약 및 치료법 개발을 지원하기 위해 Orchestra Bio를 인수한다고 밝혔습니다 [8].
- **Reservoir 농업용 로보틱스 인큐베이터 출범**: Reservoir가 WSU IAREC, WTFRC, TRIDEC과 협력해 워싱턴주 재배자를 위한 농업 로보틱스 인큐베이터를 발표했으며, 앞서 John Deere와 1,000만 달러 규모의 3년 R&D 파트너십을 체결한 바 있습니다 [16].

selectedItems.articleText: Gazebo PMC Meeting Minutes 2026-10-19 - Gazebo PMC - Open Robotics Discourse Gazebo PMC Meeting Minutes 2026-10-19 Gazebo Gazebo PMC gazebo , meeting , pmc azeey October 20, 2026, 9:03pm 1 Hi Gazebo Community! This week’s meeting was held on 2026-10-19T18:00:00Z and the following is a summary: PMC Business Approved adding Luca Della Vedova as a mentee PMC member. New agenda items Community Meeting : A reminder for this week’s community meeting on Scalable Multi-Robot Simulation in ROS 2 and Gazebo , featuring multi-robot simulation, namespaces, and automatic bridging. Please note the change in date and time this month (7:00 PM Pacific) to better accommodate the Asia-Pacific region. Fuel Server Outage & Maintenance : The Fuel server experienced downtime over the weekend due to high memory consumption triggered by crawler traffic downloading models in parallel. The server was restarted, and backend changes are being prepared to avoid loading full models into RAM along with an updated deployment mechanism (fuel-server#25 ). Auto-Merge & Required CI Checks : Maintainers are reminded to verify which CI checks are required before enabling GitHub auto-merge. A recent Fortress backport (gz-sim#4076 ) auto-merged despite failing builds because only the DCO check was required, and had to be reverted (gz-sim#4079 ). Branch protection rules are being updated in terraform_github_repos#10 to require Jenkins and GitHub Actions CI checks. Lightweight 2D Physics Engine Exploration (Box2D vs. TPE) : Discussed experimenting with Box2D as a physics engine plugin to support very large-scale planar simulations with hundreds of robots requiring only collisions and basic kinematic motion. Compared against the existing Trivial Physics Engine (TPE), which currently lacks joint support; a deeper comparison between Box2D and extending TPE will be conducted. Updates Simulation, Physics & C++20 Migration Bullet-Featherstone Kinematic Mode : Merged the full set of PRs enabling kinematic mode in Bullet-Featherstone on Rotary, with backports planned after verification on a demo world: Enforce position limits on kinematically driven joints (gz-physics#1118 ) Fix toggling links between kinematic and dynamic (gz-physics#1122 ) Kinematic base velocity for links with a CoM offset (gz-physics#1123 ) Fix force-torque sensor in hybrid kinematic/dynamic modes (gz-physics#1124 ) Fix root joint position and velocity (gz-physics#1125 ) ECM Batch Queries : Merged runtime-typed EntityComponentManager (ECM) batch queries and exposed them to Python (gz-sim#4006 ). C++20 Migration : Continuing work on gz-cmake#580 to avoid hardcoding the C++ standard so builds follow the exported target standard. PRs are in review for sdformat examples (sdformat#1733 ), gz-sim plugin examples and tutorials (gz-sim#4086 ), and the DART ContactSurface check in gz-physics (gz-physics#1134 ). Rendering, Sensors & Transport Ogre 1.12 Migration : The large Ogre 1.12 migration PR was split into stacked PRs for easier review (gz-rendering PRs ). While general custom shaders were fixed, custom terrain heightmap shaders remain broken due to upstream class removals in Ogre 1.12; the PMC agreed to merge without custom terrain shader support if a quick fix is not found, and request examples from users if needed later. PixelBuffer API Adaptations : Backports adapting gz-sensors to the PixelBuffer API (gz-sensors#674 ) have been merged for Harmonic and Fortress, and are in review for Jetty (gz-sensors#677 ) and Ionic (gz-sensors#678 ) ahead of upcoming point releases. Zenoh CI in gz-sim : A PR is in review to run Ubuntu Resolute CI tests a second time using Zenoh on gz-sim main (gz-sim#4085 ). The team agreed that gz-transport should fail explicitly when Zenoh is selected via environment variable but not compiled in, rather than silently falling back to ZeroMQ. Web & Documentation Gazebo Web Ecosystem : Ongoing work to modernize the gazebosim-app web frontend (gazebosim-app PRs ). We are also evaluating the feasibility of rewriting gzweb in Rust using the Bevy engine to improve performance, realism, and modern SDFormat support. Maintainer Guidelines : Merged documentation updates covering backport timing, downstream testing tradeoffs, and prerelease version bump review policies (docs#723 ). Infrastructure, Packaging & Release Tooling macOS 26 (Tahoe) & Homebrew : Tahoe bottling is in progress (homebrew-simulation#3599 ). The primary hurdle is compiling ogre1.9 without the Apple Graphics Library (AGL, removed in macOS 26), for which a community contributed patch is in review (homebrew-simulation#3615 ). Investigated flaky Homebrew build failures on Harmonic and Fortress caused by a Doxygen bug (homebrew-simulation#3616 ); mitigation is complete for Harmonic and in review for Fortress. Pixi on macOS : Prerequisites for supporting Pixi on macOS are in review (release-tools#1566 , release-tools#1568 ). Discussed the possibility of eventually phasing out Homebrew bottle builds if Pixi provides a smooth macOS developer experience, while keeping the Homebrew tap available. Release & CI Tooling : An automated changelog generation tool is up for review (release-tools#1447 ). A PR to skip Linux CI-pr Jenkins jobs when modified files match an ignore list is awaiting final updates (release-tools#1558 ). Build warning fixes are in review for gz-physics (gz-physics#1127 ) and gz-cmake (gz-cmake#603 ). rosdistro-extension work is underway to generate binary packages for testing distributions and handle automatic sourcing of setup.bash from child to parent workspaces. As always, the meeting notes are available at Gazebo PMC meeting weekly agenda - Google Docs . This open-source release provides offline inference with the core features needed for serving at scale. Supported models: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Supported features: Optimized kernels, model and sampler runtime Parallelism: Attention DP / balanced CP, MoE EP + EPLB DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification SWA bounded replay Asynchronous scheduling (zero-overhead batch scheduler) Batch-invariant inference Deterministic sampling Structured outputs Feature details and configuration Optimized kernels: FlashMLA , DeepGEMM , DeepEP , TileKernels , DeepSelect , and custom TileLang kernels . DSpark and confidence-scheduled verification: accelerate decoding with draft tokens and use confidence estimates to schedule verification. Set DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=1 ; DEEPINFER_USE_NEXTN_DECODE controls the maximum draft length (default: 5). Decoder SWA bounded replay: reduce decoder prefill work by replaying only a bounded suffix. Set DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_TRUNCATION_MODE=compact and DEEPINFER_YOCO_PREFILL_KEEP_TOKENS=140 for the default V4.1 settings; the retained suffix must cover the SWA window plus the maximum backtracking length. Asynchronous scheduling: overlap CPU batch scheduling with device execution. Enabled by default. Batch-invariant inference: keep model results identical across different batch compositions. Enable with DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 (NVIDIA only). Deterministic sampling: produce identical outputs for identical input tokens and sampling parameters. Set DEEPINFER_BATCH_INVARIANT=1 DEEPINFER_ENABLE_MTP_VARLEN=0 and pass a fixed seq_seed to SamplingParams (NVIDIA only). Structured outputs: constrain generation to a regex, JSON schema, or EBNF grammar. Pass so_args={"schema_type": ..., "schema": ...} to SamplingParams ; see examples . Supported hardware: NVIDIA SM100 GPUs Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs Required for a complete inference service (not included in this release): A KV cache system VE/Prefill/Decode disaggregation (most required engine functionality is already implemented) Load balancing across data-parallel replicas for both prefill and decode Getting started Prerequisites Linux GCC >= 13.0 Python 3.12 CUDA 13 (NVIDIA only) CANN 9.2 (Ascend only) Build from source Before building DeepInfer, please create and activate an empty Python 3.12 environment. # Use `ascend` instead for the Ascend platform # Keep it exported in the environment where you run DeepInfer export DEEPINFER_ACCELERATOR=nvidia ./build.sh Offline inference The default checkpoint, deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 , is downloaded into the Hugging Face cache on the first run; set DEEPINFER_HF_MODEL_DIR=/path/to/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 to run from a local copy instead. python examples/offline_inference.py See examples for details. Performance benchmarks Prefill Decode Measured on 4 SM100 GPUs for prefill and 64 for decode — each within one scale-up domain. To reproduce the benchmarks, see run_sweep.sh . Evaluation benchmarks See eval/README.md . License DeepInfer is released under the Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE for details. selectedItems.summary: Reservoir hopes to put agricultural robotics startups to work in the orchards, vineyards and berry fields alongside researchers and growers. The post Reservoir launches new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: Reservoir opened Reservoir Farms – Salinas, its flagship innovation hub. | Source: Reservoir Reservoir, Washington State University’s Prosser Irrigated Agriculture Research and Extension Center (IAREC), the Washington Tree Fruit Research Commission (WTFRC), and the Tri-City Development Council (TRIDEC) today announced a new agricultural robotics incubator for Washington growers. The site will put agricultural robotics startups to work in the state’s orchards, vineyards and berry fields alongside researchers and growers. The announcement comes as Washington growers face rising labor costs and a shrinking workforce for some of the hardest crops in the world to automate. These include apples, cherries, pears, blueberries, wine grapes, and hops. Reservoir is an agricultural innovation center and venture capital fund. The organization is focused on helping agtech startups succeed where agriculture happens, in the field. Reservoir started its innovation center in the Salinas Valley.
